pages.body:
## Overview

The two variables every mining decision hangs on: **hashprice** (revenue per unit of hashrate) and **difficulty** (the work the network demands for it). Hashprice is "a term coined by Luxor in 2019", defined as quantifying "how much a bitcoin miner can expect to earn from a specific quantity of hashrate"; the industry's canonical index is denominated per petahash-day, while Galaxy's working definition is "the market value of one unit of hashpower measured in dollars per terahash" — same quantity, three orders of magnitude apart in units. This page pins the definitions, the construction of the indexes, the October 2026 market snapshot, the difficulty/fee mechanics behind them, and the cost curve that decides who survives a down-market. Heat-first corollaries (heaters run when hashprice doesn't cover power) live in [Hashrate Heating Economics](hashrate-heating-economics.md) and [Open Mining Economics](open-mining-economics.md).

## Hashprice: two denominations, three-to-four inputs

- BTC hashprice: "a function of three inputs: block subsidy, transaction fees, and network difficulty."
- USD hashprice adds the fourth: "USD hashprice is a function of four inputs: block subsidy, transaction fees, network difficulty, and bitcoin price."
- Construction (verbatim, methodology): "Luxor's Bitcoin Hashprice Index uses a 144-block lagging simple moving average to account for transaction fees, and a simple average of the spot price for bitcoin on three US-based cryptocurrency exchanges to account for USD conversion."
- Unit (verbatim): "Luxor's Bitcoin Hashprice Index quantifies the expected value of 1 PetaHash per second (PH/s) of hashrate per day on the Bitcoin Network." Live tracking: data.hashrateindex.com; API `GET /hashprice/current`.
- Cadence: "Bitcoin's hashprice changes with every new block added to the blockchain (i.e., block height)." Difficulty, by contrast, moves on the retarget: "Network difficulty is adjusted every 2,016 blocks (approximately every two weeks) to a level that targets an average block time of ten minutes."
- Correlation rule (verbatim): "USD-denominated hashprice is positively correlated with changes to Bitcoin's spot price, block subsidy and transaction fees and negatively correlated with changes to Bitcoin's network difficulty."
- Galaxy's 2022 framing and the name analogy: "You can think of hashprice as being analogous to the value of WTI crude oil for the oil and gas industry." Galaxy separates revenue (hashprice) from survival: "breakeven hashprice, which measures the threshold below which miners begin operating unprofitably. This figure factors in operational costs like power and hosting costs, payroll (excluding any employee stock-based compensation), and selling, general and administrative (SG&A) expenses, as well as interest expense as a non-operating expense." (Galaxy open-sourced the spreadsheet calculator.)
- The Braiins *Bitcoin Mining Economics* (2023) book baseline — hashvalue/hashprice/rigprice definitions and the cost-to-mine framework — is in [Open Mining Economics](open-mining-economics.md); Luxor's index is the live-market realization of the same construct.
- Payer status: "The BTC hashprice formula is used by a majority of mining pools to pay miners for their hashrate" — i.e. FPPS/PPLNS payouts are hashprice derivatives (see [Pool Payout Schemes](../pools/pool-payout-schemes.md)).

## Market snapshot (As-Of 2026-10-10, three independent SSR sources)

| Metric | Hashrate Index homepage | WhatToMine | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hashprice | "$39.44 / PH/DAY" | — | the $/PH figure ÷ 1000 |
| BTC price | "$82,982" | "Ex. rate: $82,977.33 (WhiteBIT)" | single-venue (WTM: WhiteBIT) vs 3-exchange SMA |
| Difficulty | "Projected Difficulty 132.72 T" | "Difficulty: 132,716,002M" | current epoch 132.76T per Lookback |
| Network hashrate | "1002.42 EH/s" | "1,003,540.30 Ph/s" | same value, different smoothing |
| Block time | "9m 38s" | "9m 28s" | different windows |
| Block reward | — | "Bl. reward: 3.17" (incl. fees) | subsidy 3.125 + ~0.02–0.04 fees |
| Daily emission | — | "Daily emission: 477.809 BTC" | ≈ 144 × 3.125 + fees |

- The three sources agree within snapshot-timing variance; no dispute. WTM's multi-coin `/coins` table is JS-only (gap noted in capture); its BTC coin page and `/asics` ranking are SSR.
- Best-machine margin check from the WTM `/asics` SSR rows (at "$0.19/kWh"): "Bitmain Antminer U3S23H | Jan 2026 | 1.16 Ph/s @ 11020W | SHA-256 | $0.19/kWh | 9.50 W/Th | $49.03 | $22.58" (24h revenue/profit) — ~46% margin for the best air hardware; implied SHA-256 revenue ≈ $0.042/TH/day. Compare Luxor's energy tiers below.

## Difficulty and the 2026 network state

- September 2026 (Lookback, published 2026-10-09): "Difficulty averaged 129.24T (+2.0%), and finished the month at 132.76T. Two adjustments occurred and both were upward: +1.31% on September 5 and +4.16% on September 19, the largest single retarget since June 27."
- Hashrate trend: "the 7-day network hashrate average rose from 926 to 975 EH/s across the month"; "the 7-day hashrate average currently stands at 999 EH/s" (2026-10-08) — the 1 ZH/s threshold is live.
- Peak context (Heatmap Q4 2026, published 5 Oct 2026): "Network hashrate held at ~941 EH/s, +0.1% QoQ after -6.3% and -5.8% in the prior two quarters. It remains -8.7% year-over-year and ~15% below the ~1,110 EH/s peak set in November 2025." (Note: Heatmap counts ~941 EH/s while homepage shows 1002.42 — different metrics: country-attributed vs total.)
- Geography: "United States — 35.6% (~335 EH/s)", "Russia — 18.1% (~170 EH/s)", "China — 11.7% (~110 EH/s)" — "the top three countries commanding roughly two-thirds of global hashrate" ("65.4%, down from 66.2%").
- Fees: "Average fee collection fell 10.1% to 0.0199 BTC per block, the lowest since May. Fees were 0.63% of total block rewards, a fifteenth consecutive month below 1%." Fee revenue is noise for planning; the 144-block SMA in the index exists precisely to smooth it.
- Subsidy (methodology as written): "The block subsidy is currently 3.125 BTC" and "the next "halving" is projected for April 2028" — the docs' own double-quoted term.
- Forward curve: "Luxor's Hashrate Forward Market is pricing an average hashprice of $36.65 or 0.00044 BTC per PH/s/day over the October 2026 – March 2027 window"; September sellers locked "$30.10 and $34.72 per PH/s/day against a $39.33 spot settlement"; implied network hashrate "crosses 1 ZH/s in January 2027 at 1,029 EH".

> **Status: Disputed** — US hashrate share, two methodologies
> Cambridge DMIR 2025 survey (49 firms, 268 EH/s = "48% of the implied Bitcoin network' hashrate (as of 30 June 2024)"): "US 75.4%" of surveyed capacity (p.46–47). Luxor Heatmap (network-wide attribution, ~941 EH/s, Oct 2026): "United States — 35.6% (~335 EH/s)". Not a measurement error — firm-HQ/fleet survey coverage vs country-level hashrate attribution differ, and the dates are 15 months apart; both verbatim. Use DMIR for corporate concentration, Luxor for physical geography.

## Energy price tiers — the margin ladder (September 2026)

Luxor's Lookback publishes the electricity price each efficiency class can sustain at prevailing hashprice: "~$137/MWh for under 14 J/TH", "~$99/MWh for 14–19 J/TH", "~$74/MWh for 19–25 J/TH", "~$51/MWh for 25–38 J/TH" — against an "average industrial bitcoin mining power cost of $48/MWh".

- Read: at $39/PH/day, only machines ≤ ~25 J/TH on sub-$50/MWh power clear industrial margins — the bar home heaters beat by monetizing heat on top.
- Historical decay (DMIR, survey data): hashcost fell "$128 → $16 (−87.5%)" across epochs; BTC price "+1209%" (2020–24) against difficulty "+734%" and hashprice "−60%".
- DMIR cost curve (June 2024 survey): direct cost to mint "1 BTC" "$17,417 to $56,606, with a median of $39,189"; all-in "median of $48,333"; electricity rates median "$45/MWh" direct / "$55.5/MWh" all-in — "81.1% / 18.9%" of cash opex is electricity vs everything else.
- Hash-margin break-even matrix (DMIR p.92): "at an electricity rate of $80/MWh, miners with an efficiency of 25 J/TH are slightly above break-even, while those with 30 J/TH are already experiencing a loss"; conversely "at a lower electricity cost of $40/MWh, miners with an efficiency as low as 45 J/TH still remain profitable".

## Consumption and efficiency context (CBECI + DMIR)

- CBECI (rendered 2026-10-10): best-guess boxes 18.48 (GW) / "162.04" (TWh annualised), bounds 9.48–35.56 (GW) and 83.08–311.70 (TWh); hardware efficiency estimate "17.01 J/TH" (bounds 9.50–30.00). Model v1.4.0: release-date weighting "ranging from 1 to 0, decreasing in five steps of 0.2", five-year economic lifetime, "a delay of two months from the hardware's release date to when it is considered in our model"; 0.05 USD/kWh default; PUE 1.01/1.10/1.20; hardware basket = Bitmain/MicroBT/Canaan ("estimated combined market share of at least 85%"). Live numbers are reCAPTCHA-gated client-side; dataset pointers in the capture (full CSV not committed — no-massive-data rule).

> **Status: Disputed** — annualized consumption, CBECI vs Digiconomist (both live, Oct 2026)
> CBECI best-guess "162.04 TWh" vs Digiconomist "204.44" TWh (CBECI's own live-stats endpoint returns `{"digiconomist":"204.44"}` and methodology Table 2 carries the same anchor). The spread is methodological: CBECI models a profitability-weighted hardware fleet with PUE bounds; Digiconomist runs a continuous extrapolation. Treat 160–205 TWh as the live-methods band, not a fact discrepancy to resolve.

- DMIR 2025 (First Edition, April 2025; survey June–Sept 2024; 150 pp.): consumption "estimated at 138.2 TWh as of 30 June 2024" — "approximately 0.54% of the world's total annual electricity consumption" — with survey/CBECI cross-check "137.4 TWh"; weighted efficiency "28.2 J/TH" (−24% YoY); US 75.4% of survey hashrate (see Disputed above); energy mix "52.4% sustainable" (gas 38.2% single largest source); Bitmain 82.0% / MicroBT 15.0% / Canaan 2.1% hardware share; firmware mix: stock 44.4% / Vnish 26.4% / custom 17.6% / Braiins OS 5.6% / LuxOS 3.3% (feeds [Mining Firmware Security](../industry/mining-firmware-security.md)); 2024 divergence: hashrate "+455%" vs consumption "+111%" (2021–24).
- AI/HPC pivot (DMIR p.112–113): mining revenue "$80 to $151" per MWh vs CaaS "$1,600 to $4,000 per MWh"; CAPEX "$9 to $40 million per MW" (data center) vs "$1.2 million per MW" (mining). This is the economics driving the public-miner pivot below.

## Public miners: the 2026 repricing (TheEnergyMag, ex-TheMinerMag)

- Rebrand: theminermag.com now 301/redirects to **theenergymag.com** (same BlocksBridge/Wolfie Zhao team; "Digital Mining" section live with SSR) — the A8 "parked: JS shell" candidate cleared itself.
- Hashrate shed: "public miners lost 75 EH/s of realized hashrate while their directly reported HPC and AI revenue rose 52% quarter over quarter." At the $20/TH acquisition anchor that is "roughly $1.5 billion in equivalent hardware investment".
- Impairments: "approximately $1.1 billion in asset impairments and held-for-sale markdowns during the first half of 2026. IREN and Core Scientific (NASDAQ: CORZ) accounted for almost 89% of the total."
- Capex cycle: "Public miners and AI infrastructure peers recorded $30.7 billion of 2026 net capital spending, already 43% above their full-year 2025 total."
- Ownership datapoint (CoinShares 13F Q2 2026): "13F filers reported 264k BTC equivalent at the end of June, up from 261k in Q1 (+1.3%)"; hedge funds −22% QoQ; 13F share of US ETF AUM "rose from 20.8% to 22.4%".
- Financing pressure (CoinShares Week 41, 2026-10-09): "miners pursuing capital-intensive AI expansion remained more exposed to financing pressures and changing expectations for infrastructure returns" — with the 10Y UST "briefly reached approximately 5.36%, a 24-year high".
- Operational anchor (TheEnergyMag mining index): Bitdeer "produced 1,310 Bitcoins during the month, supported by a self-mining hash rate of 79.9 EH/s and a co-mining hash rate of 21.6 EH/s" (Aug 2026); MARA "Pledges 18,750 BTC for $600 Million New Bitcoin-Backed Loans".
- Public-miner filings economics (10-K/10-Q extract posture) is the A10 phase; this section is the press-level view.

## Firmware-as-margin (vendor-claimed)

- Braiins/GDA 40 MW case study (2026-03-03): "achieving up to 40% higher hashrate on identical hardware"; measured "the hashrate delta remained approximately 32%"; "The efficiency delta was approximately 1 J/TH". Marketing claim ("up to 40%") vs measured delta (~32%) — both verbatim, the gap is the claim's shape.
- Braiins/TÜV SÜD (2025-04-01): "greater efficiency performance in all four tests" (per-test figures context-truncated in SSR — captured as-is).
- Dashboard note: insights.braiins.com is a 1,613-byte React shell (build 8da3b47fd6f46d10, 2026-06-01); the SSR blog lives at braiins.com/blog. Hashprice widget renders label `USD/TH/Day` + "+1.53%" but the value is JS-populated — no number captured, none invented.

## Heat-reuse relevance

- The energy-tier ladder is the correct frame for heat-first deployments: home-run hardware in the "19–25 J/TH" class breaks even near "~$74/MWh" — far above the industrial "$48/MWh" average — so on residential power mining alone loses; heat monetization is the arbitrage (see [Hashrate Heating Economics](hashrate-heating-economics.md)).
- Hashprice downside is bounded work for small heaters: at "0.00048965 BTC per PH/s/day" (September's BTC-denominated average), a Bitaxe-class single-TH unit earns on the order of tens of sats per day before power — the pool-threshold math in [Pool Choice for Heat Miners](../pools/pool-choice-for-heat-miners.md) applies directly.
- Difficulty planning baseline for heater uptime (50%/yr difficulty growth assumption, sats-payback caveats) is maintained in [Hashrate Heating Economics](hashrate-heating-economics.md); this page holds the live-market side.

## See Also

- [Open Mining Economics](open-mining-economics.md) — book baselines (hashvalue/hashprice/rigprice), used-equipment price points, POD256 field data
- [Hashrate Heating Economics](hashrate-heating-economics.md) — the heat-first corollary of everything above
- [Pool Payout Schemes](../pools/pool-payout-schemes.md) — how pools actually pay the hashprice formula
- [Network State 2022–2026](../industry/network-state-2022-2026.md) — dated hashrate/difficulty/price snapshots (A10 extends)
- [Public Miner Economics](../industry/public-miner-economics.md) — filings-level view (A10)

## Overview

Practical advice the 256F community gives people getting into mining hardware and development — the lessons that repeat: plan node storage, buy the right EE books, use DigiKey's reference-designator trick, expect no single vendor to stock your BOM, and bring support requests to the forum.

## Running a node

- A Bitcoin Core node on a USB hard drive took over a month to initial-sync — plan storage accordingly [#4770 · 2026-05-05 · Skot Bitaxe]

## Learning electronics

- EE book recommendations: 'Practical Electronics for Inventors' (4th ed, Scherz) from Ryan; 'The Art of Electronics' — the classic EE book — from Skot [#4540 · 2026-03-01 · Ryan] [#4544 · 2026-03-01 · Skot Bitaxe]
- Starter passives: Amazon 0402 resistor kits recommended as the cheap way into SMD work [#5218 · 2026-07-25 · Ryan] [#5219 · 2026-07-25 · Ryan]

## Ordering parts like a pro

- DigiKey ordering trick that scales: put project reference designators in DigiKey's "customer reference" field so they print on the component bags — "HUGE. I'll fully reorder parts if they ever change"; paired lessons from the first BitaxeBIRDS order: label parts before ordering and keep overage consistent [#4269 · 2026-01-16 · Skot Bitaxe] [#4273 · 2026-01-16 · Reckless Apotheosis] [#5220 · 2026-07-25 · Skot Bitaxe]
- BOM sourcing expectations: currently impossible to fill a Bitaxe-class BOM from a single vendor (DigiKey and LCSC both come up short) and stock is a fast-moving target [#5195 · 2026-07-23 · Jayr Motta] [#5190 · 2026-07-23 · Skot Bitaxe] [#5197 · 2026-07-23 · Skot Bitaxe]

## Developing firmware from Windows

- usbipd-win + WSL guides for attaching USB devices to WSL, shared by Loren Lang [#4036 · 2026-01-04 · Loren Lang] [#4121 · 2026-01-05 · Loren Lang]
- WSL2 mechanics: Hyper-V + full Linux kernel; COM ports map to /dev/ttyS0-9 (plain serial, not USB-serial), so USB-serial discovery needs usbipd passthrough instead [#4119 · 2026-01-05 · Loren Lang] [#4035 · 2026-01-04 · Loren Lang]
- Mujina's host requirements are modest: it runs on any Linux [#3472 · 2025-11-20 · Ryan]

## Scam defense

- During the February 2026 phishing wave (fake Microsoft Teams links, RoninMiner impersonation), the AvoidCryptoScams Telegram chat got the recommendation [#4504 · 2026-02-25 · Reckless Apotheosis] [#4498 · 2026-02-25 · Deleted Account] [#4503 · 2026-02-25 · econoalchemist]

## Community etiquette

- Bring support requests to the forum rather than private channels [#5043 · 2026-07-15 · Tyler Stevens] [#5044 · 2026-07-15 · R .]

sources: bitaxeorg/ESP-Miner and bitaxeorg hardware GitHub issues, 2023-01 → 2026-10
Braiins — Bitcoin Mining Heat Reuse (Tyler Stevens, 2025)
pages.body:
## Overview

What mining silicon and hashboards can actually tolerate thermally, from practitioners who run miners as heaters and who reverse-engineer hashboards for a living. Headlines: S9-era chips are near-indestructible for heat duty; 3nm-class silicon is far less tolerant; the practical limit on hot operation is usually the secondary components (comms/analog), not the ASICs; and temperature *reporting* is unreliable enough across firmwares that field anecdotes matter as much as datasheets.

## Chip temperature limits

- Smaller-process ASICs handle hot running worse: 7nm-era chips tolerate high temps, but at 3nm the tiny channels suffer cross-channel bleed that disrupts operation — the core obstacle for high-temp heat-reuse rigs [#540 · 2024-03-21 · econoalchemist]
- Bitmain's support docs list the S9 chip temp max as 135°C [#553 · 2024-03-23 · Skot Bitaxe]; hashboard laminates get reflowed at > 220°C during assembly so the substrate is not the limiting factor, though component operating specs may drift when hot [#566 · 2024-03-23 · Skot Bitaxe]
- FutureBit designed 14nm ASICs rated to run at 110c, with prototype hashboards demonstrated boiling distilled water [#550 · 2024-03-22 · Jstefanop]
- Braiins built several hundred custom Marathon rigs from Bitmain S17 chips (BM1397) on aluminum PCBs; the custom firmware's "dangerous temp" default was 110C and efficiency around 45j per terahash; the rigs were later donated to Unbound — an aluminum PCB + 7nm chip validated as a high-temp platform [#549 · 2024-03-22 · Zack Bomsta]
- Newer Bitmain chips dropped on-die temperature sensors, so chip temp is inferred rather than measured directly like on older boards [#557 · 2024-03-23 · Skot Bitaxe]

> **Status: Disputed** — S9 practical max
> Bitmain's docs say 135°C [#553 · 2024-03-23 · Skot Bitaxe]; field experience says stock firmware reads chip temp roughly 15 degrees higher than real, so the practical max is likely only 120 [#556 · 2024-03-23 · Brett Rowan]. Best assessment: treat 135°C as the silicon's rated ceiling and ~120 as the trustworthy operating ceiling for heat-reuse duty.

## The real blocker: secondary components

- The "PCB temp" in miner readouts is an air-temperature sensor mounted on the PCB; that reading is an environment spec for secondary components, not for the laminate itself [#558 · 2024-03-23 · Brett Rowan] [#561 · 2024-03-23 · Skot Bitaxe]
- The real blocker for running silicon past the 100C mark is comms/analog parts, not the ASICs: FutureBit's high-temp test boards lasted about a week before comms/analog components began failing [#570 · 2024-03-23 · Jstefanop]
- A hashboard needs little besides ASICs and passives, which is what makes a stripped-down high-temp board plausible [#576 · 2024-03-23 · Skot Bitaxe]
- Open question raised in-community: could wide-bandgap silicon carbide / gallium nitride push chip temps past that 100C mark? [#4423 · 2026-02-13 · context thread]

## Sensor reality (EMC2101 and friends)

- EMC2101 reporting 127.875 degrees is the sensor's maximum value — a symptom of a hardware problem (short/open in the connection to the ASIC diode), not a real temperature; datasheet table 4-2 cited [#4604 · 2026-03-12 · Ryan] [#4605 · 2026-03-12 · Ryan]
- esp-miner goes through undocumented-diode setup (ideality/gain parameters) for the EMC2101 on Bitmain ASICs; Mujina users were told to check the same values [#4148 · 2026-01-06 · Skot Bitaxe] [#4151 · 2026-01-06 · Skot Bitaxe]

## Small-board (Bitaxe) thermal lessons

Bitaxes are single-digit-to-tens-of-watts boards, which makes them a clean lab for chip-level thermal behavior. Builder details (sensor wiring, fan hardware, regulator faults) live in [Bitaxe Board Design, Power & Errata](bitaxe-board-design-and-errata.md); the transferable lessons:

- **Diode readings need tuning, not averaging.** The EMC2101 reads an undocumented on-die diode, and gain/ideality must be tuned per ASIC: Gamma 600 builds "overheated" within minutes until the BM1370 readings were fixed "with better temp diode tuning on the EMC2101" ([bitaxeGamma #12](../../raw/hardware/bitaxe-osmu/2024-10-28-github-bitaxegamma-issue-12-some-bitaxegamma-builds-are-over.md)); the corrected firmware read about 10 degrees Celsius higher than before ([ESP-Miner #512](../../raw/firmware/esp-miner/2024-11-23-github-esp-miner-issue-512-chip-temperature-2-3-0-2-4-0.md)), and the GT's EMC2103 needed a -10C offset ([ESP-Miner #881](../../raw/firmware/esp-miner/2025-05-02-github-esp-miner-issue-881-need-to-tune-temperature-sensor-f.md)). Series resistance in the diode path errs by +0.7°C per ohm per the EMC2101 datasheet ([bitaxeGamma #13](../../raw/hardware/bitaxe-osmu/2024-11-03-github-bitaxegamma-issue-13-determine-proper-asic-temp-diode.md)). Chips without a die diode (BM1366) fall back to a board sensor near the ASIC, which reads cooler the farther away it sits ([ESP-Miner #1228](../../raw/firmware/esp-miner/2025-09-10-github-esp-miner-issue-1228-add-support-for-bitaxeultra-207.md)).
- **Leakage is real and measurable.** On a Supra 401 at a fixed operating point, power tracked temperature at ~0.16 W/°C; running 6 °C cooler was worth ~1 W on a 14 W board, about 3% efficiency ([ESP-Miner #1927](../../raw/firmware/esp-miner/2026-08-29-github-esp-miner-issue-1927-emc2101-fan-duty-cycle-is-scaled.md)).
- **But colder is not always faster.** One overclocked Gamma 602 lost about 100 hashrate per 5° drop; KillerInk found most of his ASICs dislike running below 60°C and drop above 65°C, while VR temperature didn't seem to matter ([ESP-Miner #1347](../../raw/firmware/esp-miner/2025-11-12-github-esp-miner-issue-1347-strange-behavior-when-surroundin.md)).
- **Fan power has an optimum.** Because fan power climbs steeply with RPM while temperature gains shrink, total system power on that Supra was flat between 76% and 85% duty and rose beyond — a controller that just chases a temperature target overshoots it. The same issue found the EMC2101 driver over-driving fans (scaling against 63 instead of 46), so naively fixing the scaling cut airflow by 27% and pushed a board from 68 °C to the 75 °C throttle point ([ESP-Miner #1927](../../raw/firmware/esp-miner/2026-08-29-github-esp-miner-issue-1927-emc2101-fan-duty-cycle-is-scaled.md)).
- **Idle is not zero.** With ASIC reset held low a Gamma still draws about 2 W — enough to make a fanless 40mm heatsink uncomfortably hot — and the fan's power-up default depends on which EMC2101 variant the assembler fitted ([bitaxe-raw #10](../../raw/hardware/bitaxe-osmu/2026-03-19-github-bitaxe-raw-issue-10-fan-default-behavior-seems-interm.md)).
- **Overheat protection pitfalls.**
  - Thresholds are guesses: ESP-Miner trips at 75 °C (ASIC) and 105 °C (TPS546 regulator) ([ESP-Miner #1099](../../raw/firmware/esp-miner/2025-06-30-github-esp-miner-issue-1099-enhancement-request-overheat-con.md)), while the OSMU FAQ's safe ranges are ASIC below 70°C and voltage regulator below 90°C ([OSMU FAQ](../../raw/hardware/bitaxe-osmu/osmu-wiki-tips-faq.md)); proposals to raise the ASIC limit lacked datasheet evidence ([ESP-Miner #316](../../raw/firmware/esp-miner/2024-09-02-github-esp-miner-issue-316-raise-overheat-limit.md)).
  - Sensor faults masquerade as heat: an open-circuit EMC2101 diode decodes to exactly 127.0 °C (compare the 127.875 maximum above), and a cached garbage regulator word caused repeated frequency downgrades that persist to NVS ([ESP-Miner #2000](../../raw/firmware/esp-miner/2026-09-25-github-esp-miner-issue-2000-overheat-protection-acts-on-sens.md)). Boot races after rapid restarts also tripped false overheat mode; invalid temps should default the fan to full ([ESP-Miner #1186](../../raw/firmware/esp-miner/2025-08-11-github-esp-miner-issue-1186-random-device-overheats-when-rap.md)).
  - Protection is silent: it lowers frequency by 100 per trip without a visible dashboard warning (open) ([ESP-Miner #1631](../../raw/firmware/esp-miner/2026-03-24-github-esp-miner-issue-1631-device-frequency-is-set-low-see.md)) ([ESP-Miner #1638](../../raw/firmware/esp-miner/2026-03-30-github-esp-miner-issue-1638-overheat-self-protect-mode-overh.md)).
  - A dead fan is the usual root cause, and an EMC2103 with no tach still reads 960 RPM and passes self-test ([ESP-Miner #1970](../../raw/firmware/esp-miner/2026-09-12-github-esp-miner-issue-1970-fan-rpm-display-will-not-move-fr.md)).
- **Mounting pressure is a thermal parameter.** Replacing the Gamma's spring clamps with M3 bolts let a user run 595MHz @ 1150mV, beyond the stock 525MHz cooler limit ([ESP-Miner #369](../../raw/firmware/esp-miner/2024-09-30-github-esp-miner-issue-369-lower-the-default-hash-frequency.md)); extra mounting holes and thicker PCBs fight board warp on multi-ASIC Bitaxes ([bitaxeGT #16](../../raw/hardware/bitaxe-osmu/2025-09-23-github-bitaxegt-issue-16-build-with-thicker-pcbs.md)).

## Cooling approaches

### Liquid cooling and cold plates

- Server-hardware research uses milled micro-jet cold plates directly over the hottest die area [#581 · 2024-03-23 · Skot Bitaxe]
- FutureBit's closed-loop micro-jet waterblocks dissipate 600 watts at 2k rpms; blocks cost $200-300 each and getting that price down is the open problem [#582 · 2024-03-23 · Jstefanop] [#585 · 2024-03-23 · Jstefanop]
- Antminer hydro hashboards only touch water blocks to the tops of the chips — nothing on the backside of the fiberglass PCB; consistent with ASIC datasheets: the large majority of heat conducts out the die surface on top [#4480 · 2026-02-21 · Skot Bitaxe] [#4481 · 2026-02-21 · Skot Bitaxe]; confirmed on S21 XPs [#4483 · 2026-02-21 · Boots Stribling]
- Skot added exposed, soldermask-free pads on board backs "just in case"; an actual rear-heatsink experiment on a Bitaxe made no difference [#4488 · 2026-02-21 · Skot Bitaxe] [#4489 · 2026-02-21 · Skot Bitaxe]
- Hydro-cooled Bitaxes run fine on plain distilled water — 'anything up to and probably including salt water' [#1435 · 2024-11-22 · Elijah Sanders]

### Immersion

- BitCool dielectric coolants are NSF-designated 'food grade' [#1813 · 2025-04-13 · Kendal Pappas]
- Karl's canola-oil immersion: no component reactions observed beyond wire-insulation stiffening; vitamin E oil added to slow oxidation; the only proof is running it until something fails [#2913 · 2025-08-16 · Karl] [#2915 · 2025-08-16 · Karl] [#2916 · 2025-08-16 · Karl]
- Gianluca (patented oil-immersion system, developed 2016-2018): 10kw dissipated in a standard 19-inch rack using only 37 L of oil, stable at 40C with 22C water in the exchanger; 3 years of 365-day immersion left hardware like new; use nylon-coated cables [#2613 · 2025-07-02 · Gianluca L] [#2629 · 2025-07-02 · Gianluca L] [#2919 · 2025-08-16 · Gianluca L] [#2920 · 2025-08-16 · Gianluca L]
- MintGreen's digital boiler / CADDY2 brochures circulated; the ~85C outlet temp attributed to their hashboard choice was questioned [#1833 · 2025-04-13 · Karl] [#1831 · 2025-04-13 · Karl]

### Thermal interface materials

- Juergen's TIM survey: squishy gap-filler pads (7.5wmk class, reusable, doesn't dry out in 6 months like Fujipoly at ~3wmk), graphite pads above 40wmk but incompressible, phase-change pads that go gooey at modest temps; 7.5wmk costs maybe only twice the cost of paste [#2903 · 2025-08-16 · Mæstro Juergen] [#2905 · 2025-08-16 · Mæstro Juergen] [#2906 · 2025-08-16 · Mæstro Juergen]
- Gianluca's endgame: gallium-indium alloy thermal pads, 75W/mK, chemically inert — better than the liquid alloy he tried first (mercury-like, very slow to apply) [#2907 · 2025-08-16 · Gianluca L] [#2908 · 2025-08-16 · Gianluca L]

### Heat-reuse thresholds

- Most absorption chillers need input heat somewhat above 80C; ~100C input enables efficient absorption chilling, opening a miner-driven heater/chiller/load-balancer appliance for buildings [#546 · 2024-03-22 · Tyler Stevens] [#590 · 2024-03-24 · Tyler Stevens]

The published book record — by this community's own author — states the same envelope from the manufacturer side ([Heat Reuse book ch. 10](../../raw/books/braiins-heat-reuse/10-innovation-ahead.md), p. 155): "Most bitcoin miners cap their device operating temperature around 80°C (176°F), a limit set by hardware manufacturers for internal electronics, not the outlet temperature of air, immersion fluid, or water used for cooling. Outlet fluid temperatures for heating from typical machines usually range between 40-70°C (104-158°F)", while "many ASIC chips are rated to operate at or above 100°C (212°F), the boiling point of water. However, the hashboards, control boards, and other sensitive electronic components have lower temperature limits, which ultimately cap the device's peak output temperature." — the print twin of the group's finding that secondary components, not silicon, set the practical ceiling. The book's appendix classifies the exhaust formally as "ultra low-grade heat, with temperatures below 100°C (212°F) – the boiling point of water" ([Heat Reuse book appendix A](../../raw/books/braiins-heat-reuse/11-appendix-a-thermodynamics.md), p. 178), and argues heat miners can spend efficiency on temperature instead: "Because the heat is valuable in addition to the bitcoin mined, marginal improvements in hashing efficiency are less important." (p. 156)

## Related hardware facts

- Antminer S19 XP hashboards use BM1366 ASICs [#371 · 2024-03-03 · Nikos]
- BM1366 chips have soldered-on heatsinks, which makes them very difficult to reuse [#4667 · 2026-04-14 · Skot Bitaxe]
- Fan-connector taxonomy: S19 XP and older use four 1x4 connectors; S19k Pro uses two 1x4 + two 2x2; S21 and newer use four 2x2 [#4448 · 2026-02-18 · Skot Bitaxe]; bitcrane PCB footprints accept either, but unsoldering is a pain [#4447 · 2026-02-18 · Skot Bitaxe]

## Purpose

This wiki separates **citations** (frozen raw captures under `raw/`) from **live endpoints** (URLs worth checking in real time). This page is the pointer table for the live layer: what each endpoint is good for, how to query it, and its house rules. Anything with numbers quoted in wiki articles should be backed by a raw capture; these pointers are for *checking current values*, not for sourcing claims.

## The pointers

| Endpoint | What it serves | How to query | Posture / contract | Wiki consumers |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **256F pool Prometheus** | Live pool/hasher telemetry: PromQL over the 256F pool's own metrics | `GET https://pool.256foundation.org/api/v1/query?query=<PromQL>` | Agent-playbook contract; the **only** sanctioned live-number source for 256F systems | Mujina fleet story, [asic-rs](../mining-software/asic-rs.md) |
| **dash.256f.org** (`hashdash`) | Tyler's dashboard — visualization only | Browser | **NOT a data source — do not scrape**; pull live numbers from the pool Prometheus endpoint above | — |
| **stratum.work** (`stratum-work`) | Live stratum message visualization per pool: real jobs, templates, Merkle branches, Sankey template flows, BIP-110 column | https://stratum.work — static chrome is prerendered; the job stream is websocket `/api/stream` (SSE per the repo) | Site = extract (chrome); live stream = session, not capture. Repo README documents collector→RabbitMQ/MongoDB→SSE architecture | [Stratum in Practice](../protocols/stratum-in-practice.md) |
| **mempool.space** (`mempool-space`) | Network/pool stats: pool share (1w/3m), difficulty, hashrate, block details | https://mempool.space/api — e.g. `/v1/mining/pools/1w` | extract; snapshot captures kept under `raw/pools/mempool/` | [Pool Centralization & FPPS](../pools/pool-centralization-and-fpps.md), [Network State](../industry/network-state-2022-2026.md) |
| **ASIC Miner Value** (`asicminervalue`) | Cross-vendor spec/profitability DB — the third-party cross-check for Bitmain/MicroBT spec tables | https://www.asicminervalue.com | extract (SSR); per-manufacturer pages | [Bitmain ASIC reference](../hardware/bitmain-asic-reference.md), hardware articles (AMV cross-checks) |
| **elektronics.dev** (`elektronics-dev`) | Rapha Zagury's curated mining dataset — "coming soon" at capture | https://elektronics.dev/about | **link-only** (no data published yet; capture on event) | this table; Phase B re-check |
| **Hashrate Index** | Hashprice spot + forward curve (Luxor) | https://hashrateindex.com — homepage numbers render SSR; API not captured | extract, snapshot only | [Hashprice and Difficulty](../economics/hashprice-and-difficulty.md) |
| **CBECI** | Cambridge network electricity estimates | https://ccaf.io/cbnsi/cbeci — live numbers need a rendered browser (reCAPTCHA-gated client-side); `/data/live` 400s to curl | documented in [CBECI landing capture](../../raw/economics/cbeci/cbeci-landing.md) | [Open Mining Economics](../economics/open-mining-economics.md) and the DMIR extract |

## Query conventions

- Every claim in this wiki cites a **raw capture**, never a live endpoint — re-run the capture if the number matters, then cite the new file.
- The pool Prometheus endpoint is the exception: it is the designated live surface for 256F operational state (dashboards, controllers) per `automation/AGENT-PLAYBOOK.md`.
- `link-only` registry rows (elektronics.dev, hashdash) exist so wiki pages can point at them without implying a verbatim capture exists.
